props.title: The Interview
props.initialSlug: Uncovering the truth, no matter the cost.

sections.content: The Interview stands as a masterclass in psychological tension, with Hugo Weaving delivering one of his pre-Matrix breakthrough performances. This Australian thriller uses the police interrogation format to create claustrophobic drama, predating similar interrogation-focused films like Prisoners (2013) and Gone Baby Gone (2007). Director Craig Monahan crafts a cat-and-mouse game that keeps viewers guessing about truth and deception, much like the later Usual Suspects (1995) but with a distinctly Australian noir sensibility.

sections.content: The film's influence can be seen in later interrogation-centered thrillers like Law Abiding Citizen (2009) and Fracture (2007), where the psychological warfare between questioner and suspect drives the narrative. The confined setting - primarily one room - creates an intensity similar to 12 Angry Men (1957), proving that compelling drama can emerge from simple setups and complex characters.

What sets The Interview apart is its exploration of truth as a malleable concept. Like Rashomon (1950) and The Usual Suspects (1995), the film plays with unreliable narrators and shifting perspectives. The interrogation becomes a chess match where each player's moves reveal and conceal in equal measure. SUBHEAD: The Evolution of Interrogation Cinema

movies.title: Identity
movies.slug: Ten strangers trapped at a motel discover they're connected in a deadly psychological puzzle

sections.content: Following The Interview, a wave of sophisticated interrogation thrillers emerged. Films like Inside Man (2006) and Compliance (2012) built on its foundation, exploring power dynamics and psychological manipulation within confined spaces. The genre peaked again with Prisoners (2013), which brought Hollywood production value to the intense interrogation format while maintaining the psychological complexity that made The Interview so compelling.
